source_text: 5.4 Τί εἴπω; τί σιωπήσω; Ἐν πλουσίοις τῆς κτίσεως θησαυροῖς ἄπορος μὲν ἡ εὕρεσις τοῦ τιμιωτέρου, δυσφορωτάτη δὲ ἡ ζημία τοῦ παρεθέντος. Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ βοτάνην χόρτου. Καὶ εὐθέως συνεξεδόθη τοῖς τροφίμοις τὰ δηλητήρια· μετὰ τοῦ σίτου τὸ κώνειον· μετὰ τῶν λοιπῶν τροφίμων ἑλλέβορος, καὶ ἀκόνιτον, καὶ μανδραγόρας, καὶ ὁ τῆς μήκωνος ὀπός. Τί οὖν; ἀφέντες τὸ ἐπὶ τοῖς χρησίμοις τὴν χάριν ὁμολογεῖν, ἐγκαλέσομεν τῷ δημιουργῷ ἐπὶ τοῖς φθαρτικοῖς ἡμῶν τῆς ζωῆς; ἐκεῖνο δὲ οὐ λογισόμεθα, ὅτι οὐ πάντα τῆς γαστρὸς ἕνεκεν τῆς ἡμετέρας δεδημιούργηται; Ἀλλ' ἡμῖν μὲν αἱ ἀποτεταγμέναι τροφαὶ πρόχειροι καὶ πᾶσιν εὔγνωστοι· ἕκαστον δὲ τῶν γενομένων ἴδιόν τινα λόγον ἐν τῇ κτίσει πληροῖ. Μὴ γὰρ ἐπειδή σοι δηλητήριον τὸ ταύριον αἷμα, τούτου ἕνεκεν ἔδει ἢ μὴ παραχθῆναι τὸ ζῷον, ἢ παραχθὲν ἄναιμον εἶναι, οὗ τῆς ἰσχύος πρὸς τοσαῦτα ἡμῶν ἐπιδεῖται ὁ βίος; Ἀλλά σοι μὲν αὐτάρκης ὁ σύνοικος λόγος πρὸς τὴν φυλακὴν τῶν ὀλεθρίων. Οὐ δήπου γὰρ πρόβατα μὲν καὶ αἶγες ἴσασιν ἀποφεύγειν τὰ κακοῦντα αὐτῶν τὴν ζωὴν, μόνῃ τῇ αἰσθήσει τὸ βλαβερὸν διακρίνοντα· σοὶ δὲ ᾧ καὶ λόγος πάρεστι, καὶ ἰατρικὴ τέχνη τὸ χρήσιμον ἐκπορίζουσα, καὶ ἡ τῶν προλαβόντων πεῖρα τῶν βλαπτόντων τὴν φυγὴν ὑποβάλλουσα, χαλεπόν ἐστιν, εἰπέ μοι, ἐκκλῖναι τὰ δηλητήρια; Ἔστι δὲ τούτων οὐδὲν ἀργῶς, οὐδὲν ἀχρήστως γεγενημένον. Ἢ γὰρ τροφὴν παρέχει τινὶ τῶν ἀλόγων· ἢ καὶ ἡμῖν αὐτοῖς παρὰ τῆς ἰατρικῆς τέχνης εἰς παραμυθίαν τινῶν ἀρρωστημάτων ἐξεύρηται. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ κώνειον οἱ ψᾶρες βόσκονται, διὰ τὴν κατασκευὴν τοῦ σώματος τὴν ἐκ τοῦ δηλητηρίου βλάβην ἀποδιδράσκοντες. Λεπτοὺς γὰρ ἔχοντες τοὺς ἐπὶ τῆς καρδίας πόρους, φθάνουσιν ἐκπέψαι τὸ καταποθὲν, πρὶν τὴν ἀπ' αὐτοῦ ψύξιν τῶν καιρίων καθάψασθαι. Ἑλλέβορος δὲ ὀρτύγων ἐστὶ τροφὴ, ἰδιότητι κράσεως τὴν βλάβην ἀποφευγόντων. Ἔστι δὲ καὶ αὐτὰ ταῦτα ἐν καιρῷ ποτε καὶ ἡμῖν χρήσιμα. Διὰ μὲν γὰρ τοῦ μανδραγόρου ὕπνον ἰατροὶ κατεπάγουσιν· ὀπίῳ δὲ τὰς σφοδρὰς ὀδύνας τῶν σωμάτων κατακοιμίζουσιν. Ἤδη δέ τινες τῷ κωνείῳ καὶ τὸ λυσσῶδες τῶν ὀρέξεων κατεμάραναν· καὶ τῷ ἑλλεβόρῳ πολλὰ τῶν χρονίων παθῶν ἐξεμόχλευσαν. Ὥστε ὃ ἐνόμιζες ἔχειν κατὰ τοῦ κτίσαντος ἔγκλημα, τοῦτό σοι εἰς προσθήκην εὐχαριστίας περιελήλυθε. 5.5 Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ βοτάνην χόρτου. Πόσην αὐτόματον λέγει τροφὴν ἐν τούτοις, τήν τε ἐν ῥίζαις, καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ βοτάνῃ, καὶ τὴν ἐν καρποῖς ἤδη; πόσην δὲ τὴν ἐξ ἐπιμελείας καὶ γεωργίας ἡμῖν προσγινομένην; Οὐκ εὐθὺς ἐκέλευσε σπέρμα καὶ καρπὸν ἀναδοθῆναι, ἀλλὰ βλαστῆσαι καὶ χλοάσαι τὴν γῆν, καὶ τότε εἰς σπέρμα τελειωθῆναι, ἵνα τὸ πρῶτον ἐκεῖνο πρόσταγμα διδασκάλιον τῇ φύσει γένηται πρὸς τὴν ἑξῆς ἀκολουθίαν. Πῶς οὖν κατὰ γένος, φησὶν, ἡ γῆ προφέρει τὰ σπέρματα, ὁπότε σῖτον πολλάκις καταβαλόντες, τὸν μέλανα τοῦτον πυρὸν συγκομίζομεν; Ἀλλὰ τοῦτο οὐχὶ πρὸς ἕτερον γένος ἐστὶ μεταβολὴ, ἀλλ' οἱονεὶ νόσος τις καὶ ἀρρωστία τοῦ σπέρματος. Οὐ γὰρ ἀπέθετο τὸ εἶναι σῖτος, ἀλλ' ἐμελάνθη διὰ τῆς καύσεως, ὡς καὶ ἐξ αὐτῆς ἐστι τῆς προσηγορίας μαθεῖν.
thought_title: Poisonous plants and the purpose of all creation
orientation: Basil is expounding the command 'Let the earth bring forth the herb of grass' and answering the objection that God created harmful plants.
pass_a_gloss: What shall I say? What shall I keep silent about? In the rich treasuries of creation, the discovery of the more valuable thing is without resource, and the loss of what has been passed over is most hard to bear. Let the earth bring forth the herb of grass. And immediately the poisons were sent out together with the foods: with the grain the hemlock; with the rest of the foods hellebore, and aconite, and mandrake, and the juice of the poppy. What then? Having left off acknowledging the grace for the useful things, shall we accuse the creator for the things destructive of our life? And shall we not reckon that, that not all things have been created for the sake of our belly? But for us the appointed foods are ready at hand and known to all; and each of the things that came to be fulfills some particular reason in the creation. For is it because bull's blood is poison to you, for this reason was it necessary either that the bull not be created, or that having been created it be bloodless, the bull whose strength our life needs for so many things? But for you the reason that dwells with you is sufficient for guarding against destructive things. For surely sheep and goats know to flee the things that harm their life, distinguishing the harmful by sense alone; but for you, for whom reason is present, and the medical art providing the useful, and the experience of those who came before suggesting the flight from harmful things, is it hard, tell me, to avoid the poisons? And of these things nothing has come to be idly, nothing uselessly. For either it provides food to some of the brute animals; or it has been discovered even for us ourselves by the medical art for the relief of certain illnesses. For the starlings feed on hemlock, escaping the harm from the poison through the construction of their body. For having narrow pores upon the heart, they manage to digest what is swallowed before the cold from it seizes the vital parts. And hellebore is food of quails, which escape the harm by the peculiarity of their mixture. And these very things are also at some time useful to us. For through mandrake doctors bring on sleep; and with opium they put to sleep the violent pains of bodies. And already some have withered the raging of appetites with hemlock; and with hellebore they have pried out many chronic afflictions. So that what you thought you had as an accusation against the creator, this has turned around for you into an addition of thanksgiving. Let the earth bring forth the herb of grass. How much spontaneous food does he speak of in these things, both the food in roots, and the food in the herb itself, and the food already in fruits? And how much the food that comes to us from care and farming? He did not immediately command seed and fruit to be sent up, but the earth to sprout and grow green, and then to be perfected into seed, so that that first command might become a teaching for nature toward the sequence that follows. How then, he says, does the earth bring forth the seeds according to kind, when having often sown wheat, we harvest this black wheat? But this is not a change to another kind, but a kind of disease and weakness of the seed. For it did not put off being wheat, but was blackened through the burning, as it is possible to learn even from the name itself.

choices.term: δυσφορωτάτη δὲ ἡ ζημία τοῦ παρεθέντος
choices.english: the loss of what has been passed over is most hard to bear
choices.why: παρεθέντος is aorist participle of παρίημι meaning 'passed over/omitted'; the loss is of what one skips or neglects, not of what is set before
rejected: the loss of what has been set before us is most hard to bear

choices.english: either that the bull not be created
choices.why: τὸ ζῷον refers back to ταύριον αἷμα, the bull whose blood is poison; the animal in question is specifically the bull
rejected: that the animal not be created

choices.english: the reason that dwells with you
choices.why: σύνοικος means 'dwelling with/alongside', emphasizing reason as a companion or housemate, not merely 'indwelling'

choices.english: in the rich treasuries of creation
choices.why: πλουσίοις modifies θησαυροῖς, both plural; 'rich treasuries' preserves the plural and the adjective-noun agreement
rejected: in the rich treasury of creation

choices.term: ἄπορος μὲν ἡ εὕρεσις τοῦ τιμιωτέρου
choices.english: the discovery of the more valuable thing is without resource
choices.why: ἄπορος means 'without resource, impossible to find a way'; the sense is that one cannot exhaust the discovery of what is more valuable
rejected: the discovery of the more valuable thing is impossible

choices.why: πυρός is wheat; the demonstrative τοῦτον points to the specific blackened wheat being discussed

pass_b_english: What shall I say? What shall I pass over in silence? In the rich treasuries of creation, the discovery of the more valuable thing is difficult, and most grievous is the loss of what has been set before us. "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass" (Genesis 1:11). And immediately the poisons were sent out together with the nourishing plants: with the grain, hemlock; with the other foods, hellebore, and aconite, and mandrake, and the juice of the poppy. What then? Shall we abandon giving thanks for the useful things and accuse the Creator for the things that destroy our life? And shall we not reckon this: that not all things have been created for the sake of our stomach? But the foods assigned to us are ready at hand and easily recognized by all; yet each of the things that came into being fulfills its own particular purpose in creation. For since bull's blood is poison to you, was it necessary for this reason either that the bull not be created, or that it be created without blood—whose strength our life needs for so many purposes? But the reason that dwells with you is sufficient for guarding against destructive things. For surely sheep and goats know how to flee from what harms their life, distinguishing what is harmful by sense perception alone; but for you, who have reason at hand, and the medical art supplying what is useful, and the experience of those who came before suggesting flight from harmful things—tell me, is it difficult to avoid poisons? And none of these things has come into being idly, none uselessly. For either it provides food for some of the brute animals, or it has been discovered by the medical art for our own relief from certain illnesses. For starlings feed on hemlock, escaping the harm of the poison through the construction of their bodies. Since they have narrow passages around the heart, they digest what they have swallowed before the chill from it can seize their vital parts. Hellebore is food for quails, which escape the harm by the peculiarity of their constitution. And these very things are also useful to us at times. For through mandrake doctors induce sleep; and with opium they lull the violent pains of the body. Some have already withered the rabid frenzy of appetites with hemlock; and with hellebore they have pried out many chronic afflictions. So what you thought you had as an accusation against the Creator has turned around for you into an increase of thanksgiving.

"Let the earth sprout the herb of grass" (Genesis 1:11). How much spontaneous food he speaks of in these words—the food in roots, and in the herb itself, and already in fruits? And how much that comes to us from care and farming? He did not command seed and fruit to be produced immediately, but the earth to sprout and grow green, and then to be perfected into seed, so that that first command might become a teacher to nature for the sequence that followed. How then, someone says, does the earth bring forth seeds according to kind, when we often sow wheat and harvest this black wheat? But this is not a change to another kind, but a kind of disease and weakness of the seed. For it has not put off being wheat, but has been blackened through scorching, as one can learn from the very name.

problems.quote: the loss of what has been passed over is most hard to bear
problems.source_quote: δυσφορωτάτη δὲ ἡ ζημία τοῦ παρεθέντος
problems.why: ζημία is 'loss/damage' but δυσφορωτάτη means 'most grievous' not 'hard to bear'; 'passed over' should be 'omitted/left aside'
problems.fix: most grievous is the loss of what has been omitted

problems.quote: most grievous is the loss of what has been omitted
problems.source_quote: δυσφορωτάτη δὲ ἡ ζημία τοῦ παρεθέντος
problems.why: παρεθέντος means 'set before us / offered,' not 'omitted.' The sense is loss of what was provided, not what was left out.
problems.fix: most grievous is the loss of what has been set before us
problems.ruling: παρεθέντος from παρίημι means 'let pass/omit,' but context demands 'set before/offered' (παρά + τίθημι sense); 'omitted' loses meaning.

problems.why: ταύριον is 'taurion,' a plant (cowbane/water hemlock), not 'bull's blood.'
problems.ruling: ταύριον αἷμα is cowbane/water hemlock poison, not literal bull's blood; mistranslation changes the meaning.

problems.quote: the bull whose strength our life needs
problems.source_quote: οὗ τῆς ἰσχύος πρὸς τοσαῦτα ἡμῶν ἐπιδεῖται ὁ βίος
problems.why: The relative pronoun οὗ refers to the animal (bull), but the argument is about the plant's utility, not the bull's strength.
problems.fix: whose strength our life needs for so many purposes
problems.ruling: οὗ refers to ταύριον (the plant), not a bull; 'bull whose strength' misreads the argument about plant utility.

dismissed.why: ἐπιδεῖται means 'stands in need of/lacks', not 'needs [it]'; the sense is 'our life lacks its strength for so many things'.

dismissed.quote: withered the rabid frenzy of appetites
dismissed.why: ὀρέξεων here likely 'urges/drives' in medical sense (rabid symptoms, not 'appetites'); λυσσῶδες suggests rabies-like symptoms, not gluttonous 'appetites'.
dismissed.note: ὀρέξεις are appetites or desires (hemlock used as an anaphrodisiac); 'rabid frenzy of appetites' is fair.
